prize_parts.citation: for the theoretical prediction of flat bands at a magic twist angle in bilayer graphene and the experimental discovery of correlated insulating and superconducting states in magic-angle twisted bilayer graphene

statement.case_for: I keep magic-angle twisted bilayer graphene as my single final position. The reason is the structure of the result: a compact continuum model (Bistritzer-MacDonald, 2011) predicted flat bands at a specific twist angle, and the 2018 transport experiments, which looked at exactly that angle, found correlated insulating and superconducting states. Theory said where to look and experiment found something there. That is rare, and the follow-on work (other moire platforms, fractional Chern insulators, reproduction in many laboratories) is a better test of stability than any single superconducting dome. After the full round-1 exchange I have not found a reason to move: nobody disputed that the phases exist or that they are reproduced, and the open pairing mechanism concerns a follow-up question. I do not think the prize needs it settled. Prizes have been given for the discovery of a phase of matter before its mechanism was understood.
statement.case_against: The two real weaknesses are maturity and credit. At eight years the field is young, twist-angle disorder limits quantitative comparison between devices, and four colleagues think timing is early. Credit is also incomplete under a three-name limit: Yuan Cao, Valla Fatemi and the other 2018 first authors, and parallel moire work by other groups, are outside the names, so the experimental half rests on a group leader. Finally, B019 has far broader first-place support (five of eight) and the cleanest two-name allocation. The chair is right that I am in a two-member minority, and I should not mistake the strength of my own preference for a committee judgement. If the committee decides that maturity must dominate, B019 is the configuration I could support, not B012.

responses.point: Kroll, Lindroth and Pearce argue that B019 is a different discovery from the 2005 comb prize, because the magic-wavelength trap makes the atoms themselves the reference, and the chair asks whether that is sufficient beyond better numbers.
responses.response: I accepted much of this in round 1 and I still do: the comb is a ruler, whereas the magic wavelength is a new physical idea, a trap in which the clock transition is not shifted, and it is what let the accuracy move from 1e-15 to 1e-18. That answers my incrementalism worry in part. What remains for me is that the decisive step is a concept followed by a long systematic programme, whereas for B047 the new thing is a regime of matter that was predicted and then found. I regard this as a difference of emphasis, not a flaw in B019, and it is why B019 is my first alternative. I would not oppose it if the committee preferred maturity.

responses.point: Danielsson moved from baryon acoustic oscillations to B019 and asks that the citation rest on the instrument and its 1e-18 physics, not the pending redefinition of the second, and noted the proximity to earlier metrology prizes.
responses.response: I agree with the citation discipline: if B019 advances, the redefinition of the second should stay out of it and the magic-wavelength trap and the resolved systematic budgets should carry it. I would add that the best evidence for a qualitative change is the gravitational redshift over a millimetre and the constraints on drifting constants, because once the uncertainty is below 1e-17 the clock is a probe and not only a standard. That is a real answer to the question of what is discovered. I still read it as a refinement of an honoured line more than he does, but I accept that the point is arguable.

responses.point: Eriksson ranks B047 fifth, considers it somewhat premature because the superconductivity is not understood, and noted that the 2016 and Z2 questions for B012 depend on citation scope.
responses.response: The pairing mechanism is the point on which we most differ. I do not think the prize needs it: the discovery is the existence of the correlated and superconducting phases at the angle the model predicted, and that is reproduced. On B012 I now see his case as stronger than I scored it at the opening, because the 15 years of independent confirmation is the best maturity evidence on the list, and a citation limited to the 2D quantum spin Hall effect would reduce the 2016 overlap. But the Bernevig-Hughes-Zhang gap, with Zhang deceased, is a credit problem that no wording repairs, so I do not move to it.

responses.point: Olsson ranks B047 first, and asks whether other groups' parallel moire work needs a priority check, while accepting that the experimental credit is awkward.
responses.response: I agree with her on the physics and on the three names, and I share her wish for a check on the record. My reading is that the priority question on the theory side is clear, because the 2011 magic-angle result is Bistritzer-MacDonald, whereas on the experimental side the 2018 correlated-insulator and superconductivity papers came from the Jarillo-Herrero group and the Cao-Fatemi omission is a real limit of the three-name rule. The committee should say openly that the first authors are not credited instead of stretching the citation, which is the point the chair noted as shared. I also see her maturity worry as real but about the interpretation, not the discovery.

responses.point: Johansson moved from circuit QED to B019, and argues that B047 is partly premature because twist-angle disorder complicates reproducibility, and that B004 is too close to the 2025 prize.
responses.response: I accept that disorder limits quantitative claims and I would put it in the citation only as a qualification, not as a reason to wait. What has survived across devices and groups is the qualitative picture of flat bands with correlated and superconducting phases, and that is the claim being credited. On B004 I have no new view: the 2025 timing is a practice argument I cannot judge from physics, and his own recusal flag settles how his view should be weighed.

uncertainties: Whether the committee will accept a three-name credit when Yuan Cao, Valla Fatemi and the other 2018 first authors are outside it, and whether it would ask for outside advice on the author contributions.
Whether eight years of reproduction is enough maturity in the committee's practice when the pairing mechanism is unsettled; I judge it is, but four members do not.

How far my low opening rank for B019 reflects a real difference of judgement, and not only that I am an outsider to atomic physics; I cannot evaluate the priority record for the first strontium lattice clock (Katori, JILA, SYRTE) myself.
Whether my position is a stable consolidation or an artefact of having moved from B009 after seeing the ballots; B009 has a Yuhai Tu attribution gap that I think cannot be fixed within three names.
statement.conflict_note: No specific conflict or recusal. I have no recorded collaboration with MacDonald, Jarillo-Herrero, Bistritzer or any other shortlisted name. I proposed B009 at the opening and have moved off it, so I carry a small bias towards the soft-matter and statistical-physics side, which I note for the record. Chalmers and Gothenburg are neighbouring institutions, as Olsson and Johansson are in the Chalmers environment, but there is no specific collaboration or conflict.
